The case analysis for the perturbed triangle shows that duplicating a pair does not increase the student's maximum beyond 4 per 7-pair block, but such “triangle” blocks are not the adversary’s optimal construction.  The true worst case is built from 4-pair blocks.

**Upper bound ($N\le 51$).**  
The adversary partitions 34 distinct positive integers into 17 pairs $(a_i,b_i)$ and, for each $i$, writes the four pairs
$$(a_i,b_i),\ (-a_i,b_i),\ (a_i,-b_i),\ (-a_i,-b_i).$$
This yields exactly $17\cdot 4=68$ pairs and respects the condition that no $k$ has both $(k,k)$ and $(-k,-k)$.  In any legal erasing the student chooses a sign for each $a_i$ and each $b_i$.  A pair in the $i$-th block is covered iff at least one of its two entries matches the erased sign.  Checking the four sign choices shows that at most **3** of the 4 pairs in each block can be covered.  Hence the student scores at most $17\cdot 3 = 51$.

**Lower bound ($N\ge 51$).**  
We show the student can always secure 51 points.  First observe that replacing any diagonal pair $(k,k)$ or $(-k,-k)$ by the tautology $(k,-k)$ can only *help* the student: for every fixed sign choice, $(k,-k)$ is always covered whereas $(k,k)$ is covered only when $k$ is erased positively.  Thus it suffices to consider boards with **no** diagonal pairs.

On such a board every pair is either a tautology $(k,-k)$ (always covered) or involves two distinct absolute values.  The student now picks, independently for each absolute value $k$, to erase all $+k$’s or all $-k$’s with probability $1/2$ each.  A pair with two distinct absolute values is then covered with probability exactly $3/4$, and a tautology with probability $1$.  If there are $t$ tautologies and $68-t$ other pairs, the expected score is
$$t+\frac34(68-t)=51+\frac{t}{4}\ge 51.$$
Hence some deterministic choice of signs scores at least 51.

Combining both bounds, the largest number the student can guarantee is

$$\boxed{51}$$
